claims.text: About 75 percent of women have at least one episode; 40 to 45 percent two or more
claims.quote: An estimated 75% of women will have at least one episode of VVC, and 40%–45% will have two or more episodes.

claims.text: Usually caused by Candida albicans, occasionally other species
claims.quote: VVC usually is caused by Candida albicans but can occasionally be caused by other Candida species or yeasts.

claims.text: Not usually acquired through sex; CDC does not recommend treating partners
claims.quote: Uncomplicated VVC is not usually acquired through sexual intercourse, and data do not support treatment of sex partners.

claims.text: Azoles relieve symptoms and clear cultures in 80 to 90 percent who complete therapy
claims.quote: Treatment with azoles results in relief of symptoms and negative cultures in 80%–90% of patients who complete therapy.

claims.text: Recurrent VVC defined as three or more episodes in less than a year; affects fewer than 5 percent
claims.quote: Recurrent VVC, usually defined as three or more episodes of symptomatic VVC in <1 year, affects <5% of women

claims.text: Weekly oral fluconazole 100, 150 or 200 mg for 6 months is the maintenance regimen
claims.quote: Oral fluconazole (i.e., a 100-mg, 150-mg, or 200-mg dose) weekly for 6 months is the indicated maintenance regimen.

claims.text: Initial therapy for recurrent VVC: 7 to 14 days topical, or fluconazole 100/150/200 mg on days 1, 4 and 7
claims.quote: (e.g., 7–14 days of topical therapy or a 100-mg, 150-mg, or 200-mg oral dose of fluconazole every third day for a total of 3 doses [days 1, 4, and 7]) is recommended

claims.text: Normal vaginal pH below 4.5 in yeast infection
claims.quote: Candida vaginitis is associated with normal vaginal pH (<4.5).

claims.text: Typical symptoms: itching, soreness, painful sex, external burning with urination, discharge
claims.quote: Typical symptoms of VVC include pruritus, vaginal soreness, dyspareunia, external dysuria, and abnormal vaginal discharge.

claims.text: Signs: vulvar swelling, cracks/fissures, thick curdy discharge
claims.quote: Signs include vulvar edema, fissures, excoriations, and thick curdy vaginal discharge.

claims.text: Saline or 10% KOH wet prep showing budding yeast, hyphae or pseudohyphae supports the diagnosis in a symptomatic woman
claims.quote: The diagnosis can be made in a woman who has signs and symptoms of vaginitis when either a wet preparation (saline, 10% KOH) of vaginal discharge demonstrates budding yeasts, hyphae, or pseudohyphae,

claims.text: KOH breaks down cell material that can hide the yeast
claims.quote: Use of 10% KOH in wet preparations improves the visualization of yeast and mycelia by disrupting cellular material that might obscure the yeast or pseudohyphae.

claims.text: Culture or PCR for complicated VVC to confirm diagnosis and identify non-albicans species
claims.quote: Vaginal culture or PCR should be obtained from women with complicated VVC to confirm clinical diagnosis and identify non–albicans Candida.

claims.text: Culture and susceptibility testing for patients who remain symptomatic; azole resistance becoming more common
claims.quote: C. albicans azole resistance is becoming more common in vaginal isolates and non–albicans Candida is intrinsically resistant to azoles; therefore, culture and susceptibility testing should be considered for patients who remain symptomatic.

claims.text: Candida on culture without symptoms is not a reason to treat
claims.quote: Identifying Candida by culture in the absence of symptoms or signs is not an indication for treatment

claims.text: About 10 to 20 percent of women carry Candida in the vagina
claims.quote: approximately 10%–20% of women harbor Candida species and other yeasts in the vagina

claims.text: Evaluate and test if symptoms persist after an OTC product or recur within 2 months
claims.quote: any woman whose symptoms persist after using an over-the-counter preparation or who has a recurrence of symptoms <2 months after treatment for VVC should be evaluated clinically and tested.

claims.text: Uncomplicated vs complicated classification (sporadic, mild to moderate, likely C. albicans, nonimmunocompromised; complicated includes recurrent, severe, non-albicans, diabetes or immunocompromise)
claims.quote: Box 4: "Sporadic or infrequent VVC" "Mild-to-moderate VVC" "Likely to be Candida albicans" "Nonimmunocompromised women" ... "Recurrent VVC" "Severe VVC" "Non-albicans candidiasis"

claims.text: Over-the-counter vaginal regimens: clotrimazole 1% 7 to 14 days, 2% 3 days; miconazole 1, 3 or 7 days; tioconazole single application
claims.quote: Clotrimazole 1% cream 5 g intravaginally daily for 7–14 days / Clotrimazole 2% cream 5 g intravaginally daily for 3 days / Miconazole 1,200 mg vaginal suppository one suppository for 1 day

claims.text: Prescription vaginal regimens: butoconazole, terconazole 0.4% (7 days), 0.8% (3 days), 80 mg suppository (3 days)
claims.quote: Terconazole 0.4% cream 5 g intravaginally daily for 7 days / Terconazole 0.8% cream 5 g intravaginally daily for 3 days / Terconazole 80 mg vaginal suppository one suppository daily for 3 days

claims.text: Oral regimen: fluconazole 150 mg single dose
claims.quote: Fluconazole 150 mg orally in a single dose

claims.text: Severe VVC defined by extensive erythema, edema, excoriation, fissures
claims.quote: Severe VVC (i.e., extensive vulvar erythema, edema, excoriation, and fissure formation)

claims.text: Severe VVC: 7 to 14 days topical azole or fluconazole 150 mg twice, 72 hours apart
claims.quote: Either 7–14 days of topical azole or 150 mg of fluconazole in two sequential oral doses (second dose 72 hours after initial dose) is recommended.

claims.text: Pregnancy: only topical azoles for 7 days
claims.quote: Only topical azole therapies, applied for 7 days, are recommended for use among pregnant women.

claims.text: Fluconazole should not be used in pregnancy, even a single 150 mg dose (miscarriage, congenital anomalies)
claims.quote: Epidemiologic studies indicate a single 150-mg dose of fluconazole might be associated with spontaneous abortion and congenital anomalies; therefore, it should not be used.

claims.text: Topical azoles: no systemic side effects, possible local burning or irritation
claims.quote: Topical agents usually cause no systemic side effects, although local burning or irritation might occur.

claims.text: Recurrent VVC idiopathic or secondary to frequent antibiotics, diabetes, other host factors
claims.quote: Recurrent VVC can be either idiopathic or secondary (related to frequent antibiotic use, diabetes, or other underlying host factors).

claims.text: Most women with recurrent VVC have no apparent predisposing condition
claims.quote: the majority of women with recurrent VVC have no apparent predisposing or underlying conditions.

claims.text: Non-albicans species in 10 to 20 percent of recurrent VVC
claims.quote: C. glabrata and other non–albicans Candida species are observed in 10%–20% of women with recurrent VVC.

claims.text: Non-albicans: 7 to 14 days of a non-fluconazole azole
claims.quote: The optimal treatment of non–albicans VVC remains unknown; however, a longer duration of therapy (7–14 days) with a nonfluconazole azole regimen (oral or topical) is recommended.

claims.text: Boric acid 600 mg gelatin capsule vaginally once daily for 3 weeks if non-albicans infection recurs
claims.quote: 600 mg of boric acid in a gelatin capsule administered vaginally once daily for 3 weeks

claims.text: Specialist referral if symptoms recur
claims.quote: If symptoms recur, referral to a specialist is advised.

claims.text: Immunocompromised women may not respond as well to short courses
claims.quote: and those receiving immunosuppression therapy (e.g., corticosteroid treatment) might not respond as well to short-term therapies.

claims.text: Male partners: a minority have balanitis with redness of the glans and itching or irritation
claims.quote: A minority of male sex partners have balanitis, characterized by erythematous areas on the glans of the penis in conjunction with pruritus or irritation.

claims.text: No substantial evidence for probiotics as treatment
claims.quote: No substantial evidence exists to support using probiotics or homeopathic medications for treating VVC.

claims.text: Short-course topical formulations treat uncomplicated VVC
claims.quote: Short-course topical formulations (i.e., single dose and regimens of 1–3 days) effectively treat uncomplicated VVC.
